    Constellation Energy Generation, LLC                                                EL25-20
                                                                                   (Consolidated)
    v.

    PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.


          Request for Clarification of Eolian LP, Antora Energy LLC, and Verrus LLC

           Pursuant to Rule 212 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“Commission” or “FERC”), 1 Eolian L.P. (Eolian), Antora Energy LLC,

and Verrus LLC request clarification of the Commission’s December 18 Order in the above-

captioned proceeding (Order). Specifically, the undersigned parties ask the Commission to

clarify that where the Order provides that a Co-Located load may “request only the minimum

level of interconnection service it deems necessary to effectuate its Co-Location Arrangement,” 2

that it means the Co-Located Load may nominate a net withdrawal limit in the same manner that



1
    18 C.F.R. § 385.212.
2
    Order at P 232.


                                                      2
 it may nominate a net injection limit. Making this clarification will ensure that Co-Located loads

paired with energy storage can use their full technical capabilities to avoid unnecessary network

upgrades, thereby advancing the Commission’s twin goals of protecting ratepayers and

advancing speed-to-power within PJM.

         The Commission’s order is a big step forward in delivering a commonsense solution to

growing demand. As Commissioner Rosner explains, it does so by “enabl[ing] large loads to

reduce how much they lean on the grid, while ensuring that they pay their fair share.” 3 In the

Order, the Commission found PJM’s tariff unjust and unreasonable because it does not include

transmission service reflecting that some Co-Located Loads “are willing and able to limit their

energy withdrawals from the transmission system.” 4 The Commission found that extending new

transmission service options is necessary to ensure that Co-Located Loads pay only for the

services they use, and also to ensure that Co-Located Loads use their ability to limit withdrawals

to avoid “costly and inefficient transmission system buildout.” 5 The Commission’s logic should

compel complementary reforms to the generator interconnection process, because that process

also may evaluate withdrawals from the Co-Located Load and therefore may also result – absent

clarification – in “costly and inefficient transmission system buildout.”

         The Commission should make clear that PJM must enable interconnection customers to

nominate withdrawal limits in the interconnection process, just as it requires PJM to allow

generators to limit their proposed output. Accurate modeling of withdrawals is particularly

critical to the ability of Co-Located Loads incorporating energy storage to connect without

triggering transmission upgrade needs. Due to their unique technical capabilities and ability to



3
  Id. at P 4.
4
  Id. at P 177.
5
  Id.


                                                     3
 deploy quickly, energy storage is an essential piece of the solution to enabling timely connection

of large electricity customers. While energy storage currently comprises a small portion of the

overall resource mix in PJM, there are many projects in development and storage is an integral

piece of multi-technology solutions for large customers. The Commission’s Order is an important

step in enabling such solutions but without clarification, ambiguity in how such solutions are to

be studied in the interconnection process could continue to stymie their development.

I.      BACKGROUND


        A.       Energy storage resources are critical for meeting data center loads quickly
                 and reliably


        Energy storage resources are positioned to play a critical role in meeting demand from

new large loads, especially co-located data center loads. A key reason is that batteries are

uniquely well suited to respond to the minute-to-minute volatility of data center loads. Natural

gas turbines and reciprocating engines can play an important role in providing energy to a Co-

Located Load, but are not capable of following the highly volatile load profiles of AI data

centers, and risk damage when they do. 6 For these reasons, battery storage is being deployed

across a range of data center applications, including many that also incorporate thermal

generation.

        Energy storage resources are also faster to deploy and can meet the aggressive schedules

of data center loads. For example, 7,722 MW of the 26,618 MW selected in PJM’s RRI were




6
  Authors from Siemens Energy note” “In large data centers, demand swings can reach 100 MW or more, occurring
multiple times per minute on sub-second timescales. . . The unpredictable demand profile created by these transients
can be challenging for gas turbines or reciprocating engines, which are designed for relatively stable baseload
operation. . . .Even the most advanced droop control governing in gas turbines cannot handle the rapid changes in
frequency. If left unmitigated over time, severe damage can occur, shortening the lifespan of gas turbine units.”
Danny Clayton and Nico Jansen van Rensburg, Pipeline & Gas Journal (Dec. 1, 2025).


                                                              4
 from batteries. 7 And, of the “new” projects selected in the RRI (as opposed to uprates), all but

one of the projects scheduled to deploy this decade are batteries. 8 Market rules that do not utilize

storage to its full capabilities will necessarily slow progress.

        The Order is premised in no small part on the concept that Co-Located loads can manage

their total withdrawals from the grid, and that their capability to do so should be enabled to

reduce overall system costs. Energy storage resources are better positioned than any other

resource to manage the total withdrawals from a Co-Located load quickly and reliably. As

Constellation explained in this docket, using battery energy storage systems to provide backup

service at data centers “can supply a consistent level of energy for several hours,” allowing a

developer to “minimize costs related to system design.” 9

        B.       Request for Clarification


        Clarification is necessary to realize the Commission’s intent of ensuring that Co-Located

Loads do not pay for services that they do not use and do not trigger network upgrades that they

do not need. The Commission’s order requires PJM to establish rules for Interconnection

Customers serving co-located load, 10 both for new service requests, 11 and for modifications to

existing facilities through the necessary study process. 12 For both processes, we seek clarification

that interconnection customers serving co-located load must be permitted to nominate net

initiative---summary-results.pdf.
8
  The lone exception is the Three Mile Island restart, which was in planning well before selected in the RRI. See,
PJM, Reliability Resource Initiative Additional Summaries (May 6, 2025) at 6 – 8, available at
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/committees/pc/2025/20250506/20250506-rri-addendum-
--post-meeting.pdf.
9
  Answer of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, at 98-99 (April 23, 2025).
10
   Order at P 187.
11
   Id. at PP 231-236.
12
   Id. at PP 225-230.


                                                            5
 withdrawal limitations for purposes of these interconnection study processes. 13 The

Commission’s order requires PJM to develop transmission service frameworks that allow

customers to take curtailable service based on the use of special protection schemes that enable

reliable, curtailable service based on technical and engineering requirements set by PJM, 14 and

requires PJM to enable an interconnection customer to request the “minimum level of

interconnection service it deems necessary.” 15 We seek clarification that, as applied to an

interconnection request by a Co-Located Load that includes energy storage components, this

means that to the extent PJM performs study steps involving withdrawal assumptions from both

the storage facility components and the co-located load components, these study steps must

allow the interconnection customer to provide for limits to the injection and withdrawal rights for

the generation and co-located load facilities reflecting the proposed integration of those facilities.

                 1.       The order’s requirements and necessary clarification

        The Commission’s Order finds that “the PJM Tariff is unjust and unreasonable because it

lacks sufficient clarity and consistency with respect to the rules for Co-Location Arrangements”

and on this basis directs changes to the new service request process, as well as the necessary

study process for modifications to existing facilities. With regard to “Interconnection Customers

seeking to use new generating facilities to serve Co-Located Load,” the Commission requires

PJM to clarify that it “shall consider requests for interconnection service below the full

generating capability of the generating facility, so that an Interconnection Customer may request

interconnection service at a level below its maximum facility output to serve Co-Located




13
   See Comments of Bloom Energy Corporation at 11 (requesting an interconnection study process that limits net
load impacts to “the nominated net grid withdrawal” of the co-located facilities).
14
   Order at P 212.
15
   Id. at P 232.


                                                            6
 Load.” 16 The Order specifies that “[t]his revision will clarify that an Interconnection Customer

seeking to use a new generating facility to serve a Co-Located Load may request only the

minimum level of interconnection service it deems necessary to effectuate its Co-Location

Arrangement.” 17 With regard to the necessary study process, the Commission requires PJM “to

add to the Tariff a description of the scope of the analysis that it will perform as part of the

necessary study process when an Interconnection Customer seeks to use its existing generating

facility to serve Co-Located Load,” which must include a description of “the information that the

Interconnection Customer must provide about the Co-Located Load for purposes of the

necessary study.” 18

        While these directives from the Commission make clear that an interconnection customer

must be able to request service below a generator’s full output capability, they do not explicitly

address how PJM must modify its tariff with regard to the study assumptions used for

interconnection requests involving energy storage resources co-located with loads. With energy

storage resources, the assumptions that PJM uses for purposes of the resource’s withdrawals

from the grid are an important part of the study process. PJM’s study process sets forth rules for

how withdrawals from energy storage facilities will be modeled, and PJM recently submitted a

compliance filing in Docket No. ER24-2045 to effectuate the Commission’s requirement in

Order No. 2023 to use operating assumptions in interconnection studies that reflect the proposed

charging behavior of electric storage resources. 19 Missing from that framework, however, is a

description of whether and how such studies may factor in co-located load when a co-located

generation facility is proposed. To fill that gap, the Commission should require that, to the extent


16
   Order at P 232.
17
   Id.
18
   Id. at P 227.
19
   See PJM Transmittal Letter, Docket No. ER24-2045, at 39-42 (Oct. 22, 2025).


                                                            7
 that PJM includes the co-located load in such studies, 20 it must allow the interconnection

customer to provide withdrawal limits for both the energy storage resource components and the

co-located load. This clarification should apply to both new interconnection service request study

processes, as well as the necessary study process. Further, just as the Commission requires “PJM

to describe the information that the Interconnection Customer must provide about the Co-

Located Load for purposes of the necessary study,” 21 the Commission should also require PJM to

specify what information about the Co-Located Load is required for purposes of the new service

request study process. As Antora previously explained, without such information, any process

that includes the impact of the proposed load may not capture the proposed “load shape and

flexibility,” or account for special protection schemes proposed to be integrated into the co-

located facilities. 22 In other words, the Commission should clarify that PJM must not include

overlapping load and energy storage withdrawal impacts in its generator interconnection study

process unless it does so accurately, based on information about both the load and storage

components of the facility, and the proposed net withdrawal limits of the facility. Without such

direction, there is a risk that imprecise or inaccurate modeling assumptions will identify network

upgrades that are not needed to integrate the proposed facilities with the grid.




20
   We recommend that the Commission avoid necessarily requiring the co-located load to be modeled as part of such
studies, as the decision whether to include load may depend on the timing of the load interconnection request study
processes vis-à-vis the generation interconnection request; and the question of whether and how the load is modeled
may implicate complex questions concerning the interaction between the load and generation interconnection
processes. However, the Commission should require that, to the extent that load is included within the generation
interconnection study assumptions, it must be incorporated in a manner that allows for the interconnection customer
to provide for joint withdrawal limits between the storage and load components, based on the facility’s capabilities
and plan for operation, as supported by information about the generation resource and load submitted by the
interconnection customer.
21
   Order at P 227.
22
   Motion to Intervene Out of Time and Comments of Antora Energy LLC In Response to the Commission’s Co-
location Order, at 9-10 (April 23, 2025).

                  2.      Clarification is required in order to ensure just and reasonable rates

        The Order finds the existing PJM tariff unjust and unreasonable because it lacks clear

provisions to govern the “rates, terms, and conditions of service that apply to Interconnection

Customers serving Co-Located Load and Eligible Customers taking transmission service on

behalf of Co-Located Load.” 23 The requested clarification aims to address precisely this defect:

the absence of clear rules that govern how co-located load paired with storage will be studied in

the generator interconnection process. The PJM tariff, as currently drafted, does not specify how

storage withdrawals will be modeled when a storage facility is seeking to co-locate with a large

load.

        This absence of clear tariff provisions means that without clarification, there is a risk that

the interconnection study process could include assumptions that the load and the charging load

of the storage resource create bluntly overlapping grid impacts (e.g. coincident withdrawals at

peak), when in fact the storage resources and co-located load could be managed to limit the

overall withdrawal of the co-located resource and to avoid withdrawal when doing so would

create grid impacts necessitating network upgrades. The record demonstrates that interconnection

customers can build facilities that integrate a variety of “onsite self-supply resources—such as

fuel cells, gas turbines, or battery storage” and use “controls and protection mechanisms” such

that the integrated facility “can limit maximum flows into and out of” co-located facilities. 24 Yet

as Bloom Energy Corporation explains, PJM’s tariff has “no existing protocols” for studying new

generation (including energy storage) together with load. 25




23
   Order at P 175.
24
   Comments of Bloom Energy Corporation, Attachment, Brattle Report at 9, 27 (April 23, 2025).
25
   Comments of Bloom Energy Corporation at 10.


                                                           9
          The Order recognizes that co-located resources can be integrated so as to “limit [the]

energy withdrawals” of co-located loads so as to prevent “inefficient and costly transmission

buildout.” 26 But it does so in the context of requiring PJM to offer non-firm transmission service,

without expressly applying this reasoning to the interconnection study context. In requiring PJM

to offer co-located loads a menu of transmission service options, the Order ensures that such

loads have the opportunity to receive service that “reflect[s] their actual impact on the

transmission system.” 27 But the value presented by the option to obtain non-firm transmission

service would be substantially diminished if the generator interconnection process separately

forces the co-located load to bear the cost and delay of unnecessary network upgrades that do not

“reflect[s] their actual impact on the transmission system.” 28 The Commission should clarify that

its findings in requiring non-firm service also apply with regard to PJM’s interconnection study

processes, as this is the process that directly identifies necessary transmission upgrades. The

Commission must require PJM to allow for non-firm withdrawal and integrated operation of co-

located facilities including net withdrawal limits to be integrated into interconnection study

assumptions because failing to do so “could necessitate inefficient and costly transmission

buildout.” 29

         While the Order’s clear intent is to protect customers from unnecessary upgrade costs, 30

the path to realizing billions in transmission infrastructure savings enabled by facilities that

incorporate “controls and protection mechanisms used to limit physical withdrawals” is to reflect

the controllable nature of those withdrawals in interconnection studies that identify the need for




26
   Order at P 199.
27
   Id. at P 162.
28
   Id.
29
   Id. at P 199.
30

                                                     10
 transmission upgrades. 31 By expressly requiring PJM to allow interconnection customers seeking

to use new generating facilities to serve Co-Located Load to nominate net withdrawal limits, the

Commission will enable the avoidance of unnecessary upgrades and allow for the faster

integration of new customers and a more affordable grid.

           The Order permits a co-located generator to nominate an injection limit that is less than

its total capacity. 32 The requested clarification is the logical extension of that principle to

withdrawals and would result in the same benefits of avoided costs and faster interconnection

times. Conversely, study assumptions that ignore the joint capabilities of energy storage

resources paired with co-located loads paired would frustrate the objectives of the Order and

render its replacement rate ineffectual for those resources. Allowing co-located loads paired with

storage to nominate withdrawal limits will encourage innovation that will bring down these

costs. It will allow developers to optimize the configuration of load, generation and storage in a

way that internalizes impacts to the transmission system, bringing down overall system costs and

accelerating speed to power.
